newsitem.title: YEMEN: Yemeni kidnappers change minds on German hostages.
newsitem.headline: Yemeni kidnappers change minds on German hostages.

text.p: Seven German tourists seized by Yemeni tribesmen were still held hostage on Wednesday despite reports of their release on Tuesday, a Yemeni official said.
"The kidnappers changed their mind at the last minute yesterday," the official told Reuters. "The negotiations have been resumed again."

The German embassy referred all calls about the week-long incident to the foreign ministry in Bonn, where spokesman Martin Erdmann said the men had not arrived in Sanaa as expected, which meant that their released must have been delayed.

Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel instructed the German ambassador in Sanaa, Helga Strachwitz, to request an immediate meeting with President Ali Abdullah Saleh to try to shed light on the hostages' situation.

The seven men, aged between 30 and 45, were kidnapped by tribesmen last week while riding motorcycles through the Wadi al-Dabaat area between Mahra and Hadramaut, some 770 km (480 miles) to the east of the capital.
A Yemeni security official said on Tuesday the kidnappers had agreed to release the Germans after security forces and troops tightened a siege on them.
A German embassy spokesman told Reuters on Tuesday the seven tourists were in good health and the ambassador thanked the Yemeni authorities for their safe release.

Kinkel issued a statement thanking Yemeni security forces for insuring the men's release and also expressing appreciation of the roles of officials in the Yemeni foreign and defence ministries and in the provincial capital Mukallah.

The Yemeni security official had said last-minute negotiations had centred on the tribesmen's demand of a government amnesty in return for releasing their hostages. The official declined to say whether any of the demands had been met.
Kidnapping is a common ploy by tribesmen holding grievances against the government or foreign oil firms operating in Yemen, one of the Arab world's most impoverished countries.

Dozens of tourists, diplomats and other foreigners have been seized in recent years. The tribesmen have tried to use the foreigners, who have included a U.S. diplomat and a Saudi ambassador, as bargaining chips.
Siege by security forces has been the usual government response.
In the latest incident, the tribesmen wanted to pressure the government to bring to justice an alleged Yemeni swindler who sold them cars smuggled from Gulf Arab states.
